headline: Dry weather with a cooling trend lasts through the weekend, then a strengthening storm fed by a weak to locally moderate atmospheric river (a long plume of Pacific moisture) is increasingly likely to bring heavy rain, possible thunderstorms, strong winds and a flash-flood risk Tuesday into Wednesday.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Friday was the last very warm day west of the mountains. High clouds increase overnight, which should keep low coastal clouds from becoming widespread, though patchy low clouds around 700 to 1,200 feet are possible late tonight (about a 25 percent chance near San Diego and 15 percent near Santa Ana). Saturday brings more high clouds and cooling as the high pressure weakens and a storm passes well to the north, mainly in the western valleys, where highs drop into the 70s to near 80.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Cooling spreads inland toward the mountains Sunday, with stronger ocean breezes and breezier conditions in the mountains and deserts, where mountain highs stay in the 50s and 60s. Light showers become more likely late Sunday night into Monday morning, but most areas from the coast to the coastal mountain slopes get about a quarter inch or less. Temperatures cool to within about 5 degrees of normal under cloudier skies Monday.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Heavier rain arrives late Monday night or Tuesday morning as a rapidly deepening storm pulls in a weak to locally moderate atmospheric river, sweeping northwest to southeast Tuesday and ending sometime Wednesday morning or afternoon; models are unusually consistent on timing this far out. Early estimates are 1 inch or more and locally near 3 inches west of the mountains (highest in the LA basin), around half an inch in the lower deserts with some spots over an inch, and higher totals in the high desert; an unstable atmosphere and warm ocean water raise thunderstorm chances and the risk of flash flooding, and strong winds are expected, most impactful near the coast, though speeds are uncertain. Snow levels start above 8,000 feet Tuesday morning and fall to around 6,000 feet, bringing a chance of snow showers to the San Bernardino Mountain villages. After a brief dry break later Wednesday into early Thursday, the unsettled pattern continues and a weak low pressure system may bring more cool, wet weather late next week.

coast: High tides keep dropping this weekend, to around 7 feet Saturday and below 7 feet Sunday, running about a foot above normal predictions; Saturday morning's high tide plus elevated surf brings minor to locally moderate coastal flooding. A reinforcing long-period west swell arriving overnight builds surf Saturday to 4 to 7 feet with sets to 8 feet on exposed west-facing beaches and near piers, highest in the morning and early afternoon, under a Beach Hazards Statement for the Orange and San Diego County coasts through Saturday afternoon. No hazardous boating conditions are expected through Monday, but southwest winds build Tuesday with widespread gusts of 30 to 35 knots (about 35 to 40 mph) Tuesday morning through Wednesday morning, steep, choppy seas, a 20 to 30 percent chance of storm-force gusts Tuesday morning and afternoon, and a slight chance of thunderstorms on the water Tuesday.
watch_for: Rain totals and thunderstorm/flash-flood risk with Tuesday–Wednesday's storm, which could still shift in track and strength
Strong winds Tuesday, especially near the coast
Minor to locally moderate coastal flooding and big surf Saturday morning
confidence: Forecasters are confident in the dry, cooling weekend and unusually confident this far out in the timing of the Tuesday–Wednesday storm, with growing confidence in heavy rain, but exact rain totals, wind speeds and impacts remain uncertain, as does the weather late next week.
